gloss: The activity of chasing and killing wild animals for food or sport.
examples: *Hunting* is a big part of life in that part of the state.
He gave up *hunting* after his knees went bad.
Deer *hunting* brings a lot of money into small towns every fall.

gloss: The activity of catching fish with a line, a net, or a trap.
examples: We went *fishing* off the pier on Saturday morning.
The *fishing* is better early, before the sun hits the water.
My grandfather taught me everything I know about *fishing*.

gloss: Someone who hunts wild animals.
examples: A *hunter* found the missing hiker on the ridge.
Thousands of *hunters* head into the woods on opening weekend.
She's a better *hunter* than anyone else in the family.

gloss: Someone who catches fish, for a living or for sport.
examples: My uncle is a commercial *fisherman* out of Gloucester.
Two *fishermen* pulled the kayaker out of the water.
Every *fisherman* on that lake knows where the good spots are.
contrast: The plural *fishermen* sounds almost the same as the singular — the difference is only in the middle vowel, so listen for the article.

gloss: Food put on a hook or in a trap to attract fish or animals.
examples: We stopped for gas and a box of *bait*.
The fish stripped the *bait* right off the hook.
He uses corn as *bait* for catfish.

gloss: One trip or occasion of hunting animals.
examples: They're planning an elk *hunt* in Montana this fall.
The morning *hunt* ended with nothing but wet boots.
He's been on a dozen *hunts* and never fired a shot.

gloss: The fish that someone has caught, or the amount caught.
examples: We cleaned the *catch* on the dock before dark.
That's a nice *catch* for one afternoon.
Their *catches* have gotten smaller every year.

gloss: A long flexible stick with a reel, used to catch fish with a line.
examples: He got a new *fishing rod* for his birthday.
Three *fishing rods* were leaning against the truck.
Don't leave the *fishing rod* in the sun all day.

gloss: A simple rod for fishing, often a plain one without a fancy reel.
examples: The kids each had a cheap *fishing pole* from the hardware store.
He carried a *fishing pole* over his shoulder like a rifle.
We keep a couple of *fishing poles* in the garage.
contrast: In everyday American speech *pole* and *rod* mean the same thing; *pole* just sounds more casual.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The thin strong cord that runs from a reel to the hook.
examples: I need to put new *fishing line* on this reel.
A bird got tangled in some *fishing line* on the shore.
Two *fishing lines* crossed and made a mess.

gloss: The equipment used for fishing, such as rods, hooks, and lures.
examples: All my *tackle* is in the back of the truck.
He spent a hundred dollars on *tackle* and caught nothing.
Good *tackle* lasts a lifetime if you take care of it.
contrast: In football a *tackle* is countable, but fishing *tackle* never takes -s.

gloss: An artificial bait made to look like something a fish wants to eat.
examples: That silver *lure* works great in muddy water.
He must have fifty *lures* in that box.
I lost my favorite *lure* on a log.

gloss: A small sharp bent piece of metal used to catch fish.
examples: He got a *fishhook* through his thumb and needed stitches.
A handful of *fishhooks* had rusted in the bottom of the box.
Tie the *fishhook* on with a good knot.

gloss: A small weight that pulls a baited hook down into the water.
examples: Add a *sinker* if you want the bait to stay on the bottom.
The current is strong, so use heavier *sinkers*.
My *sinker* snagged on a rock and the line broke.

gloss: A small float on the line that dips under when a fish bites.
examples: Watch the *bobber* — it went under twice already.
The kids like the red and white *bobbers*.
Set the *bobber* about three feet above the hook.
contrast: Americans say *bobber*; the British call the same thing a *float*.

gloss: A box with trays for carrying hooks, lures, and other fishing gear.
examples: His *tackle box* weighs more than the fish he catches.
There are two old *tackle boxes* up in the attic.
Everything goes back in the *tackle box* before we leave.

gloss: A net on a handle used to lift a hooked fish out of the water.
examples: Grab the *landing net* — this one's big.
He forgot the *landing net* and lost the fish at the boat.
Rubber *landing nets* are easier on a trout's skin.

gloss: A mesh of cord used to catch fish in large numbers.
examples: The crew hauled in the *fishing net* by hand.
Old *fishing nets* wash up on this beach all winter.
A seal tore a hole in the *fishing net*.

gloss: A boat used for catching fish.
examples: A small *fishing boat* was anchored just off the point.
The *fishing boats* come back into the harbor around four.
He bought a used *fishing boat* with a bad motor.

gloss: A journey made in order to go fishing.
examples: We're taking a *fishing trip* up to Minnesota in July.
Their yearly *fishing trips* go back thirty years.
The whole *fishing trip* got rained out.

gloss: Someone who fishes with a rod and line, especially for sport.
examples: The river draws *anglers* from all over the country.
A patient *angler* will do better on this stretch.
State rules require every *angler* over sixteen to carry a license.

gloss: Fishing with a rod, line, and hook as a sport.
examples: *Angling* is the most popular outdoor sport in the county.
The magazine covers fly *angling* in the West.
He wrote a whole book about *angling* for bass.

gloss: An official document that allows a person to hunt legally.
examples: You can buy a *hunting license* online in about five minutes.
The warden asked to see our *hunting licenses*.
His *hunting license* expires at the end of the month.
contrast: American English spells the noun *license*; British English spells it *licence*.

gloss: An official document that allows a person to fish legally.
examples: A one-day *fishing license* costs about fifteen dollars here.
Kids under sixteen don't need *fishing licenses*.
Keep your *fishing license* in your wallet, not in the boat.

gloss: The period of the year when hunting a particular animal is allowed.
examples: Deer *hunting season* runs from November to early January.
The state sets different *hunting seasons* for each animal.
He takes vacation every year during *hunting season*.

gloss: The period of the year when fishing for a certain species is allowed.
examples: Trout *fishing season* opens the last Saturday in April.
Bad weather ruined half the *fishing season*.
The two *fishing seasons* overlap by about a week.

gloss: The stretch of time when it is legal to hunt or catch a certain animal.
examples: It's *open season* on coyotes year-round in this state.
*Open season* for ducks starts in the middle of October.
The *open seasons* are printed in the back of the regulations booklet.

gloss: The first day of a hunting or fishing season.
examples: Half the town takes off work on *opening day*.
We were on the water at dawn on *opening day*.
*Opening days* are always crowded at this lake.

gloss: The largest number of animals or fish one person may legally take in a day.
examples: The daily *bag limit* is six birds.
*Bag limits* change from one county to the next.
We hit our *bag limit* before nine in the morning.

gloss: An officer who enforces hunting and fishing laws.
examples: A *game warden* checked our licenses at the boat ramp.
*Game wardens* patrol the whole river during the spawn.
She's been a *game warden* for twelve years.

gloss: Someone who hunts or fishes illegally.
examples: A *poacher* shot the deer out of season and got caught.
*Poachers* work at night with spotlights.
The ranch hired guards to keep *poachers* off the land.

gloss: The crime of hunting or fishing without the right to do so.
examples: *Poaching* carries a heavy fine in this state.
He lost his license for three years for *poaching*.
Elephant *poaching* has dropped in some countries.

gloss: A model of a bird set out on the water to draw real birds within range.
examples: We set out two dozen *decoys* before sunrise.
One *decoy* had come loose and drifted off.
He carves wooden *decoys* in the winter.
contrast: The noun is usually stressed on the first syllable (DEE-koy); as a verb the stress often moves to the second (di-KOY).

gloss: A small shelter where hunters hide while waiting for ducks.
examples: We sat in the *duck blind* for four hours in the rain.
He built a *duck blind* out of scrap lumber and reeds.
The *duck blinds* along that marsh are all rented out.
contrast: Americans call this a *blind*; the British word for the same thing is a *hide*.

gloss: A seat or platform fixed up in a tree for a hunter to watch from.
examples: He climbed into the *tree stand* before it got light.
Always wear a harness in a *tree stand*.
Two *tree stands* overlook the far end of the field.

gloss: A device that catches and holds an animal.
examples: He set a *trap* by the creek for beaver.
Her dog got a paw caught in a *trap*.
The *traps* are checked every morning by law.

gloss: A loop of wire or cord that tightens around an animal that walks into it.
examples: He set a wire *snare* on the rabbit run.
*Snares* are illegal for most animals in this state.
The fox pulled the *snare* loose and got away.

gloss: Someone who catches animals in traps, usually for their fur.
examples: An old *trapper* lived alone up that valley.
*Trappers* opened up much of the West before the settlers came.
He works as a *trapper* for the county in the spring.

gloss: The practice of catching animals with traps.
examples: *Trapping* season runs through the coldest months.
He learned *trapping* from his father.
The state requires a separate permit for *trapping*.

gloss: A bird that people are allowed to hunt, such as a duck or a quail.
examples: Pheasant is the most popular *game bird* around here.
The refuge raises *game birds* and releases them each fall.
You need a stamp to hunt any migratory *game bird*.

gloss: Large wild animals such as deer, elk, and bear that people hunt.
examples: He's hunted *big game* on three continents.
*Big game* tags are handed out by lottery.
The rifle is heavy enough for *big game*.

gloss: Small wild animals such as rabbits and squirrels that people hunt.
examples: A .22 is plenty for *small game*.
*Small game* season opens in September.
Most kids around here start out hunting *small game*.

gloss: Meat from wild animals that have been hunted.
examples: The freezer is full of *game meat*.
*Game meat* is leaner than beef.
She has a great recipe for stew with *game meat*.

gloss: An area of land where people hunt.
examples: That ridge has been their family *hunting ground* for generations.
The new highway cut right through the best *hunting grounds*.
He knows every acre of this *hunting ground*.

gloss: Protected land set aside where wild animals can live and breed.
examples: The *wildlife refuge* floods its fields every fall for the ducks.
Hunting is allowed in parts of some *wildlife refuges*.
We drove out to the *wildlife refuge* to watch the geese come in.

gloss: Someone hired to look after game animals on private land.
examples: The estate employs a *gamekeeper* and two assistants.
*Gamekeepers* feed the birds through the winter.
The *gamekeeper* met us at the gate.
contrast: Mainly British; the American officer who enforces hunting law is a *game warden*.

ru: вредный зверёк (койот, сурок и т. п.)
gloss: A wild animal treated as a pest, such as a coyote or a woodchuck.
examples: He keeps a rifle in the truck for *varmints*.
Some *varmint* got into the chicken coop last night.
*Varmint* hunting has no closed season here.
contrast: A country pronunciation of *vermin*; it stays informal.

gloss: The route that migrating birds follow every year.
examples: This marsh sits right on the Mississippi *flyway*.
The four main *flyways* run north and south across the country.
Duck numbers along the *flyway* are up this year.

gloss: A dog bred and trained to help people hunt.
examples: A good *hunting dog* is worth more than the gun.
His two *hunting dogs* ride in the back of the truck.
She trains *hunting dogs* on the side.

gloss: A dog trained to find and flush game birds.
examples: That *bird dog* can smell a quail fifty yards off.
*Bird dogs* need a lot of running to stay in shape.
He paid a fortune for a trained *bird dog*.

gloss: A dog trained to work alongside a hunter with a shotgun.
examples: A steady *gun dog* doesn't move until you send it.
He breeds *gun dogs* out of a kennel in Kansas.
The *gun dog* sat perfectly still through the whole volley.

gloss: A dog trained to bring back birds that a hunter has shot.
examples: The *retriever* swam out and brought back both ducks.
*Retrievers* love cold water more than any other breed.
Their black *retriever* is twelve years old and still works.

gloss: A hunting dog that freezes and points its nose at hidden birds.
examples: The *pointer* locked up at the edge of the corn.
He runs two *pointers* on the prairie every October.
A good *pointer* holds until the hunter walks in.

gloss: A long-haired hunting dog that points at game birds.
examples: His English *setter* works close in thick cover.
The two *setters* covered the whole field in an hour.
That *setter* has the softest mouth of any dog he's owned.

gloss: A small hound with drooping ears, used mainly to hunt rabbits.
examples: You can hear the *beagles* running the brush from a mile off.
He hunts rabbits behind a pair of *beagles*.
Our *beagle* follows her nose everywhere.

gloss: A strong fixed-blade knife used to skin and cut up game.
examples: He carries a *hunting knife* on his belt.
A dull *hunting knife* is more dangerous than a sharp one.
Two *hunting knives* came with the set.
contrast: The k in *knife* is silent, and the plural is *knives*, not 'knifes'.

gloss: A cartridge holding many small pellets, fired from a shotgun.
examples: He loaded three *shotgun shells* and snapped the gun shut.
A box of *shotgun shells* costs more every year.
An empty *shotgun shell* was lying in the grass.

gloss: Large lead pellets fired from a shotgun at big animals.
examples: He loaded *buckshot* for deer in thick brush.
The sign was full of holes from *buckshot*.
*Buckshot* is illegal for deer in some counties.

gloss: Small lead or steel pellets fired from a shotgun at birds.
examples: Use *birdshot* for dove and quail.
A little *birdshot* peppered the far end of the field.
Steel *birdshot* is required for waterfowl.

gloss: A small telescope mounted on a rifle to help the shooter aim.
examples: He put a new *scope* on the deer rifle.
Fog on the *scope* cost him the shot.
Cheap *scopes* lose their zero after a few shots.
contrast: Also an everyday word meaning range or extent ('the scope of the project'), and in that sense it is uncountable.

gloss: A small telescope on a stand, used to look at distant animals.
examples: He glassed the far slope with a *spotting scope*.
*Spotting scopes* are heavy to carry up a mountain.
Set the *spotting scope* on a tripod so it stays steady.

gloss: A small device that measures how far away a target is.
examples: The *rangefinder* said two hundred and ten yards.
Modern *rangefinders* work through light rain.
He never shoots without checking the *rangefinder* first.

gloss: An old-style gun loaded with powder and a ball through the front of the barrel.
examples: There's a separate season for *muzzleloaders*.
He hunts with a *muzzleloader* his grandfather built.
A *muzzleloader* gives you one shot and no more.

gloss: The old kind of gunpowder used in muzzleloaders.
examples: *Black powder* makes a huge cloud of white smoke.
He measures the *black powder* by hand for each shot.
The *black powder* season starts a week before rifle season.

gloss: The backward push a gun gives when it is fired.
examples: That shotgun has a lot of *recoil*.
A pad on the stock soaks up some of the *recoil*.
She flinched from the *recoil* and missed high.

gloss: A narrowing at the end of a shotgun barrel that controls how the shot spreads.
examples: Use a tighter *choke* for longer shots.
The gun came with three screw-in *chokes*.
An open *choke* is better in close cover.

gloss: A heavy locked cabinet for storing firearms.
examples: Everything goes back in the *gun safe* when we get home.
*Gun safes* are required if you have kids in the house.
It took four men to move the *gun safe* into the basement.

gloss: Bullets and shells, in everyday informal speech.
examples: We're low on *ammo* for the .30-06.
*Ammo* got expensive after the shortage.
He keeps his *ammo* in a locked box under the bed.
contrast: Short for *ammunition*; both are uncountable — never 'ammos'.

gloss: A place set up for people to practice shooting safely.
examples: We sighted in the rifles at the *shooting range*.
The county opened two new *shooting ranges* last year.
The *shooting range* closes at dusk.

gloss: A sport in which people shoot at clay targets thrown across their path.
examples: He shoots *skeet* every Sunday morning.
*Skeet* is good practice for duck season.
The club holds a *skeet* tournament in June.

gloss: A flat disk thrown into the air as a target for shotgun practice.
examples: He broke nineteen *clay pigeons* out of twenty.
A *clay pigeon* sailed out over the pond.
We went through three boxes of *clay pigeons*.

gloss: Someone who shoots very accurately.
examples: His grandfather was a fine *marksman*.
The club is full of serious *marksmen*.
You don't have to be a *marksman* to hunt turkey.
contrast: The plural *marksmen* sounds nearly the same as the singular; only the middle vowel differs.

gloss: The bright orange color hunters wear so other hunters can see them.
examples: State law says you have to wear *blaze orange* during deer season.
His vest and hat are both *blaze orange*.
You can spot *blaze orange* through the thickest brush.

gloss: The sport or skill of shooting with a bow and arrows.
examples: *Archery* season comes before the rifle season.
She took up *archery* in high school.
The camp teaches *archery* to kids every summer.

gloss: A short bow set across a stock, fired like a gun.
examples: He hunts deer with a *crossbow* now that his shoulder is bad.
*Crossbows* are legal here during the whole archery season.
The *crossbow* is heavier than it looks.

gloss: A case for carrying arrows.
examples: He pulled another arrow from his *quiver*.
The *quiver* clips right onto the bow.
Both *quivers* were empty by the end of practice.

gloss: A wide sharp arrow point used for hunting animals.
examples: He screwed a fresh *broadhead* onto the arrow.
*Broadheads* have to be razor sharp.
A dull *broadhead* wounds an animal instead of killing it.

gloss: The practice of hunting with trained hawks or falcons.
examples: *Falconry* takes years of training and a special permit.
He got interested in *falconry* after a demonstration at the fair.
*Falconry* is one of the oldest field sports there is.

gloss: Someone who keeps and hunts with trained birds of prey.
examples: The *falconer* held the hawk on a thick leather glove.
There are only a few dozen licensed *falconers* in the state.
A *falconer* has to feed the bird by hand every day.

gloss: A hunt in which riders on horses follow a pack of hounds after a fox.
examples: The club holds a *fox hunt* every Thanksgiving morning.
She rode in her first *fox hunt* at fourteen.
*Fox hunts* still draw a crowd in parts of Virginia.

gloss: A small wooden or plastic whistle blown to imitate a duck.
examples: He blew the *duck call* twice and the flock turned.
Wooden *duck calls* sound warmer than plastic ones.
Learning a *duck call* takes a whole season.

gloss: A device used to imitate the sound of a wild turkey.
examples: He worked the *turkey call* until a gobbler answered.
There are a dozen kinds of *turkey calls* in that box.
A bad *turkey call* will spook every bird in the woods.

gloss: A block or patch of salt that wild animals come to lick.
examples: Deer come to the *salt lick* at dusk.
He put out two *salt licks* along the fence line.
Using a *salt lick* to draw deer is illegal in some states.

gloss: A camera strapped to a tree that takes pictures when an animal walks past.
examples: The *trail camera* got three pictures of the same buck.
He has *trail cameras* on every trail on the property.
The *trail camera* ran out of batteries in the cold.

gloss: A narrow path worn through the woods by wild animals.
examples: We followed a *game trail* down to the creek.
*Game trails* cross the whole hillside.
His stand looks right down a *game trail*.

gloss: The smell an animal leaves behind, which dogs follow.
examples: The hounds picked up a *scent* near the river.
Rain washes the *scent* right off the ground.
Wind carried our *scent* straight to the deer.
contrast: The c is silent: *scent*, *sent*, and *cent* all sound the same.

gloss: The droppings of a wild animal, used to tell what has passed by.
examples: There was bear *scat* right on the trail.
You can tell a lot from *scat* — what it ate and how long ago.
The guide pointed at some fresh *scat* by the stream.

gloss: The mating season when male deer chase females and lose their caution.
examples: The *rut* usually peaks around the second week of November.
Bucks move all day during the *rut*.
He takes his vacation to hunt the *rut*.
contrast: Also an everyday word for a deep groove worn in a dirt road, or a dull routine.

gloss: The shaking excitement a hunter feels when a big animal finally appears.
examples: He got *buck fever* and forgot to take the safety off.
*Buck fever* has cost more deer than bad shooting.
Even after thirty years he still gets a touch of *buck fever*.

gloss: The job of cleaning out a killed animal right where it fell.
examples: *Field dressing* a deer takes about twenty minutes.
He learned *field dressing* from his uncle.
Do the *field dressing* fast so the meat cools.
contrast: In first aid a *field dressing* is a bandage — same words, completely different thing.

gloss: The dead body of an animal.
examples: We hung the *carcass* in the shed to cool.
Coyotes had gotten to the *carcass* overnight.
The *carcasses* go to the processor in town.
contrast: British writing sometimes spells it *carcase*; American English uses *carcass*.

gloss: An animal that a hunter or predator has killed.
examples: The wolves stayed near the *kill* for two days.
It was a clean *kill* at a hundred yards.
He's had only two *kills* all season.

gloss: The craft of preparing and stuffing dead animals so they look alive.
examples: He does *taxidermy* out of a shop behind his house.
Good *taxidermy* isn't cheap.
She took a class in *taxidermy* at the community college.

gloss: Someone whose job is mounting animal skins to look lifelike.
examples: The *taxidermist* said it would take six months.
There are only two *taxidermists* left in the county.
He dropped the antlers off at the *taxidermist*.

gloss: A business or person that supplies guides and gear for hunting or fishing trips.
examples: We booked the trip through a local *outfitter*.
The *outfitter* provides horses, tents, and meals.
Several *outfitters* work out of that little town.

gloss: Someone who hunts or fishes for sport and follows the rules of fair play.
examples: The club is open to any *sportsman* in the county.
*Sportsmen* pay for most of the state's conservation work.
A real *sportsman* doesn't shoot a sitting bird.

ru: любитель охоты, рыбалки и жизни на природе
gloss: Someone who spends a lot of time hunting, fishing, and camping.
examples: Her father was a lifelong *outdoorsman*.
The store is full of gear for *outdoorsmen*.
You don't have to be a serious *outdoorsman* to enjoy the trip.

gloss: A fish big enough by law to be kept instead of thrown back.
examples: That one's a *keeper* — right at fifteen inches.
We caught thirty fish and maybe four *keepers*.
Anything under the limit goes back; only *keepers* go in the cooler.

gloss: The practice of putting every fish back in the water after catching it.
examples: This whole stretch of river is *catch-and-release*.
He's practiced *catch-and-release* since he was a kid.
*Catch-and-release* keeps the big fish in the system.

gloss: A light careful bite from a fish that does not take the hook.
examples: I got a *nibble* but nothing set.
We sat there two hours without a single *nibble*.
A few *nibbles* means the bait is too big.

gloss: The amount of fish or game brought in at one time.
examples: That's the biggest *haul* we've had all summer.
The boat came in with a poor *haul*.
Their *hauls* have dropped off since the new rules.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *hall* (a corridor or a large room).

gloss: The moment at a tournament when the fish are put on the scale.
examples: The *weigh-in* starts at three o'clock at the dock.
He missed the *weigh-in* by four minutes.
Big crowds show up for the *weigh-ins*.
contrast: *Weigh* sounds exactly like *way*.

gloss: A cord or chain used to hold caught fish in the water beside you.
examples: He had five bluegill on the *stringer*.
Keep the *stringer* in the shade so the fish stay fresh.
A turtle got into one of our *stringers*.

gloss: A basket that an angler carries caught fish in.
examples: He came back with three trout in his *creel*.
Old wicker *creels* sell as antiques now.
She lined the *creel* with wet grass.

gloss: A pole with a big hook, used to pull a large fish into a boat.
examples: Hand me the *gaff* — I can't lift him by the line.
The mate sank the *gaff* into the tuna.
Two *gaffs* hung on the wall of the cabin.
contrast: Sounds like *gaffe* (an embarrassing social mistake), which is a different word.

gloss: A small metal link that lets the line turn without twisting.
examples: Tie a *swivel* between the line and the leader.
A pack of *swivels* costs a couple of dollars.
The *swivel* keeps the lure from spinning up your line.

gloss: The small backward point on a hook that keeps a fish from slipping off.
examples: Pinch the *barb* down with pliers before you fish here.
The *barb* went in past his knuckle.
Hooks without *barbs* are easier to take out.

gloss: A hook with three points joined on one shank.
examples: That lure has two *treble hooks* on it.
A *treble hook* is hard to get out of a fish's mouth.
He swapped the *treble hooks* for single ones.

gloss: Clear single-strand nylon line used for fishing.
examples: He spooled the reel with ten-pound *monofilament*.
*Monofilament* stretches more than braided line.
Sunlight makes old *monofilament* brittle.

gloss: A weighted hook with a soft or hairy body, bounced along the bottom.
examples: A white *jig* works well in that river.
He tipped the *jig* with a piece of minnow.
She keeps a whole tray of *jigs* in different colors.

gloss: A lure with a small blade that spins and flashes as it is pulled through the water.
examples: A small gold *spinner* is all you need for these trout.
*Spinners* work best in moving water.
The *spinner* caught the light and a fish hit it right away.

gloss: Bits of fish thrown in the water to draw fish toward a boat.
examples: The mate threw *chum* over the side every few minutes.
A slick of *chum* trailed behind the boat.
*Chum* brings in sharks along with everything else.
contrast: Also an old informal word for a close friend, and it sounds exactly the same.

gloss: A large earthworm used as fishing bait.
examples: We picked *nightcrawlers* off the lawn after the rain.
One *nightcrawler* is plenty for a hook that size.
Keep the *nightcrawlers* in the refrigerator overnight.

gloss: A very small fish, often used alive as bait.
examples: We bought a bucket of *minnows* at the bait shop.
A single *minnow* on a hook will catch a crappie.
*Minnows* were flickering in the shallows.

gloss: A young fish about the size of a finger.
examples: The hatchery released ten thousand *fingerlings* into the river.
A trout *fingerling* takes two years to reach legal size.
The pond was stocked with *fingerlings* last spring.

gloss: The eggs that fish lay in the water in great numbers.
examples: *Spawn* was stuck to the weeds all along the shallow end.
The salmon die soon after they leave their *spawn*.
Cold water slows the *spawn* down by a couple of weeks.

gloss: A place where fish eggs are raised until the young fish can be released.
examples: The state *hatchery* stocks this lake every April.
Most of these trout came out of a *hatchery*.
Budget cuts closed two *hatcheries* last year.

gloss: An area or industry where fish are caught commercially.
examples: The cod *fishery* collapsed in the early nineties.
New rules are meant to keep the *fishery* healthy.
Both *fisheries* are closed until the stock recovers.

gloss: A set of steps built beside a dam so fish can swim upstream.
examples: You can watch salmon climb the *fish ladder* from a window.
The dam was rebuilt with a *fish ladder*.
Old *fish ladders* were too steep for most species.

gloss: The act of throwing a baited line out over the water.
examples: *Casting* into the wind takes practice.
He spent an hour on the lawn working on his *casting*.
Long *casting* isn't necessary on a small creek.

gloss: Fishing by dragging a baited line slowly behind a moving boat.
examples: *Trolling* along the drop-off got us two lake trout.
*Trolling* covers a lot of water in a short time.
He does most of his *trolling* early in the morning.
contrast: Spelled and said the same as internet *trolling* — the fishing sense came first.

gloss: A small quiet electric motor that moves a boat slowly while fishing.
examples: He ran the *trolling motor* along the weed line.
The battery for the *trolling motor* died halfway through.
New *trolling motors* hold the boat in place by themselves.

gloss: Waterproof boots joined to trousers, worn for standing in a river.
examples: My *waders* sprang a leak at the knee.
He pulled on his *waders* and stepped into the current.
A good pair of *waders* will last several seasons.
contrast: Always plural, like *pants*: one garment is still *waders*, or *a pair of waders*.

gloss: A paved slope where boats are backed into the water off a trailer.
examples: There was a line of trucks at the *boat ramp*.
Both *boat ramps* on this side of the lake are free.
Ice closed the *boat ramp* until March.

gloss: A small flat light boat used for fishing in shallow water.
examples: The guide poled the *skiff* across the flats.
Two *skiffs* were pulled up on the sand.
A *skiff* draws only a few inches of water.

gloss: An engine that hangs on the back of a small boat.
examples: The *outboard* wouldn't start until the third pull.
He bought a used twenty-horse *outboard*.
Older *outboards* burn a mix of gas and oil.

gloss: A low fast boat with open casting decks, built for freshwater fishing.
examples: He pulls a *bass boat* behind his pickup.
*Bass boats* filled the ramp before daylight.
The *bass boat* has a live well built into the deck.
contrast: The fish *bass* is said /bæs/, rhyming with *pass*; the musical *bass* is said /beɪs/.

gloss: A boat with a captain that people hire for a day of fishing.
examples: We took a *charter boat* out for half a day.
The *charter boats* leave the harbor at six.
A *charter boat* costs about six hundred dollars for six people.

gloss: An electronic screen on a boat that shows fish and the bottom below.
examples: The *fish finder* showed a school at twenty feet.
Modern *fish finders* draw a picture of the bottom.
He can't fish without a *fish finder* anymore.

gloss: Fishing through a hole cut in the ice of a frozen lake.
examples: *Ice fishing* doesn't start until the lake freezes solid.
He took the boys *ice fishing* over Christmas break.
*Ice fishing* is more about sitting still than casting.

gloss: A tool with a spiral blade for drilling a hole through ice.
examples: He cut four holes with a hand *auger*.
Gas *augers* go through a foot of ice in seconds.
The *auger* blade needs sharpening.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *augur* (to be a sign of something coming).

gloss: A small store selling live bait and simple fishing supplies.
examples: The *bait shop* opens at four in the morning.
Ask at the *bait shop* where they're biting.
Half the *bait shops* on this road have closed.

gloss: A store that sells rods, reels, lures, and other fishing gear.
examples: The man at the *tackle shop* tied the knot for me.
There's a good *tackle shop* just off the highway.
Local *tackle shops* know more than any website.

gloss: Fishing with a very light artificial fly cast on a heavy line.
examples: *Fly fishing* looks harder than it is.
He drove to Montana for a week of *fly fishing*.
*Fly fishing* is mostly about reading the water.

gloss: A long thin springy rod made for casting an artificial fly.
examples: He broke the tip off his *fly rod* in the car door.
Bamboo *fly rods* sell for a fortune.
A nine-foot *fly rod* handles wind better.

gloss: An artificial fly that floats on the surface of the water.
examples: A trout came up and took the *dry fly*.
He ties his own *dry flies* through the winter.
Grease the *dry fly* so it keeps floating.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The fine end section of line that the fly is tied to.
examples: Add a foot of lighter *tippet* and try again.
He carries three spools of *tippet* in his vest.
A heavy *tippet* will spook fish in clear water.

gloss: The craft of making artificial flies out of feathers, fur, and thread.
examples: *Fly tying* gets him through the winter months.
The shop offers a *fly tying* class on Thursdays.
*Fly tying* takes good eyes and steady hands.

gloss: Catching fish underwater with a spear or a spear gun.
examples: *Spearfishing* is popular off the reefs down there.
He took up *spearfishing* after he learned to free-dive.
*Spearfishing* is banned in the marine park.

gloss: The activity of catching crabs with traps, lines, or nets.
examples: We go *crabbing* off the bridge every August.
*Crabbing* is best on an incoming tide.
A chicken neck on a string is all you need for *crabbing*.

gloss: The activity of digging clams out of sand or mud at low tide.
examples: *Clamming* is only allowed at certain beaches.
We went *clamming* with rakes and a bucket.
The town sells a season permit for *clamming*.

gloss: A long net that hangs straight down and is drawn through the water.
examples: They dragged a *seine* across the shallow end of the cove.
*Seines* catch everything, big and small.
He uses a small *seine* to collect bait.
contrast: Rhymes with *sane*; the ei is not said 'ee'.

gloss: A net hung in the water that catches fish by the gills as they swim into it.
examples: *Gill nets* are banned in most inland waters here.
The crew set a *gill net* across the channel.
A seal got tangled in the *gill net*.

gloss: A boat that catches fish by dragging a big net behind it.
examples: A rusty *trawler* was tied up at the far pier.
*Trawlers* work these banks all winter.
He spent two seasons on a shrimp *trawler*.

gloss: A cage lowered to the sea floor with bait inside to catch lobsters.
examples: He hauls two hundred *lobster traps* a day.
A stack of old *lobster traps* sat behind the shed.
Each *lobster trap* is marked with a colored buoy.

gloss: A long spear with a rope on it, thrown at large sea animals.
examples: The old man kept a *harpoon* lashed to the deck.
Swordfish are still taken with *harpoons* off this coast.
He threw the *harpoon* and missed by a foot.

gloss: A freshwater fish with big glassy eyes, prized for eating.
examples: We caught a five-pound *walleye* at dusk.
*Walleyes* feed best in low light.
Fried *walleye* is on every menu up north.

gloss: A small flat freshwater fish caught in schools around brush.
examples: The *crappie* are stacked up around that sunken tree.
He filled a bucket with *crappies* in an hour.
A tiny jig is all you need for *crappie*.
contrast: Said KRAH-pee, not like the word *crappy*.

gloss: A small round freshwater fish common in ponds all over the country.
examples: Kids catch *bluegills* off the dock all summer.
A worm under a bobber will always get a *bluegill*.
The pond is full of stunted *bluegills*.

gloss: Any small freshwater fish big enough to fry whole in a pan.
examples: We kept a mess of *panfish* for supper.
*Panfish* are the easiest thing for a beginner to catch.
One good *panfish* barely covers a plate.
contrast: The plural is *panfish*, unchanged — never 'panfishes'.

gloss: A rainbow trout that goes to the sea and comes back up the river to spawn.
examples: He hooked a *steelhead* below the falls.
*Steelhead* run these rivers in late winter.
A wild *steelhead* has to be released.
contrast: The plural is usually *steelhead*, unchanged.

gloss: A big ocean fish with a long pointed bill, hunted by sport fishermen.
examples: He fought the *marlin* for three hours.
*Marlin* are tagged and released in most tournaments.
A blue *marlin* can weigh over a thousand pounds.
contrast: The plural is usually *marlin*, unchanged.

gloss: A large silver fish of warm shallow seas that jumps hard when hooked.
examples: A *tarpon* rolled right beside the boat.
*Tarpon* move up the coast in May and June.
Almost nobody keeps a *tarpon* anymore.
contrast: The plural is usually *tarpon*, unchanged.
